name: Uma Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead an underground crew in the city centre, so I'm mostly not up poles, I'm down in vaults and manholes under the streets. The big office towers and the hospital are fed by cables down there, and when a joint fails we go in, pump out the water, and splice a new section. A splice on a big cable can take a whole shift, and you have to be clean and patient, one bit of dirt and it fails in a year. I like the quiet down there, weirdly. What wears me out is the traffic control, having buses squeeze past the hole all day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does splicing involve, for someone who's never seen it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: You're joining two thick cables so the power flows through like it's one. You strip back the layers, clean everything, fit the connector, then build the insulation back up in the right order. My partner Leo is an electrician in commercial buildings, and he still says my splices look like jewellery, which is a nice thing to hear after eight hours in a wet hole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds pretty likely, honestly. Lots of noise, not much change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, the hype was bigger than the result. At work I'd say the cables still need splicing. Online I'd probably not bother saying anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means nothing changes. Good job, good pay, and Leo and I keep saving for a house. Nobody's sending a chatbot down a flooded manhole on Station Road at six in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going like I am. We'd keep putting money aside for a deposit, we've got a good chunk saved already. Maybe I'd use the AI tool a bit for checking cable specs, since that sometimes saves me a call to the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, basically. Normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use an AI tool for cable specs. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One of the younger guys showed me. You take a photo of the cable marking, and it tells you the type and the right splice kit. It's right most of the time, but I still check the book before I cut anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the next big thing for you and Leo, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A house, probably a small one near the river where it's cheaper. We'd get married at some point too, but no rush. This picture doesn't change any of that.

S0.say: She'd say it's what she expected and the hype was bigger than the result, telling colleagues the cables still need splicing. She wouldn't bother saying anything online.
S0.think: Nothing changes for her; she keeps a good job and pay and keeps saving for a house with Leo. No chatbot is going down a flooded manhole.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and keeps saving with her partner for a house deposit. Uses the AI tool a bit more to check cable specs before cutting.
S0.quote: Nobody's sending a chatbot down a flooded manhole on Station Road at six in the morning.
S0.fieldNote: Uma is grounded and practical, proud of her careful splicing. She uses AI in a small, checked way, after a colleague showed her. Her plans with Leo, a small house near the river, are untouched by this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I can see that one. It's probably already started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should get trained on whatever comes in, so we're not left behind. To friends I'd say it'll be bumpy but most people will be okay. I'd keep it balanced, I don't like doom posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job changes but doesn't go. The robots might do the pumping and the cable pulling, but splicing in a wet vault is fiddly. If a robot takes over the pumping and leaves me the splicing, honestly, I'd send it flowers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a couple of crews had tried the new kit, then sign up for the training. I'd use the AI tools more, for planning and paperwork. Money-wise, we'd keep saving for the house, maybe a bit more carefully, just in case Leo's work shifts. In the first year, I'd want to understand the new systems well enough to train my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe save a bit more carefully. What would you cut, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the holiday we were planning, a week by the sea. We'd do a shorter one, or put it off a year. It's not panic, it's just being sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo, a little. A lot of his work is wiring new offices, and if the AI changes how buildings get designed, his side might change faster than mine. He'd be fine, but it'd be stressful for him.

S1.say: She'd tell her crew to get trained so they aren't left behind and tell friends it'll be bumpy but most people will be okay. She keeps it balanced and avoids doom posts.
S1.think: Her job changes but doesn't go: robots might do pumping and cable pulling but not fiddly splicing. She'd happily hand over the pumping.
S1.do: Signs up for training once a couple of crews have tried the new kit and uses AI tools more for planning and paperwork. Keeps saving for the house, a bit more carefully, possibly shortening a planned holiday.
S1.feel: Mostly fine and a bit careful.
S1.quote: If a robot takes over the pumping and leaves me the splicing, honestly, I'd send it flowers.
S1.fieldNote: Uma is pragmatic and steady, waiting for others to test the new kit before she trains. She'd even welcome robots taking the grunt work. Her mild worry is for her partner's electrical work, which she thinks might change faster than hers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. That's scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's not panic, let's see what the company says. To friends I'd say it's big but we'll figure it out. I wouldn't post anything until I knew more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd both be in trouble, me and Leo. If robots can splice and AI can design buildings, our two good jobs could go at the same time. We've been saving for a house for three years, and suddenly I'd be wondering if we should keep the deposit as a lifeboat instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, we'd put the house on hold. We'd keep the deposit as savings, it's about a year of living costs for both of us. I'd cut back on spending, no holiday, no new car. I'd try to stay with the company as long as possible, maybe moving to whatever team checks the robots. And we'd talk about whether to put off the wedding plans too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like a cable fault you can hear but can't find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leo the night you realised it was really happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're okay for now, we've got the savings, nothing's on fire yet. Then we'd sit on the floor with a pizza and argue about whether to sign on the house anyway. He'd want to, I'd want to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning take away, compared with more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Any chance to switch properly. I'd still be figuring out what's happening when it arrives. I'd just be holding on.

S2.say: She'd tell colleagues not to panic and wait for the company's word, and tell friends it's big but they'll figure it out. She wouldn't post until she knew more.
S2.think: She and Leo could lose two good jobs at once if robots can splice and AI can design buildings. Their house deposit would turn into a lifeboat.
S2.do: Puts the house purchase on hold and keeps the deposit, about a year of living costs for both, as savings. Cuts spending, tries to stay with the company in a robot-checking role, and talks with Leo about delaying wedding plans.
S2.feel: Anxious, like a cable fault you can hear but can't find.
S2.quote: We've been saving for a house for three years, and suddenly I'd be wondering if we should keep the deposit as a lifeboat instead.
S2.fieldNote: The household angle drives Uma's reaction: two trade incomes exposed at once. Her public line stays calm while privately she's rethinking the house and wedding. She pictures a concrete night with Leo, arguing over whether to sign on the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but I can work with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a plan, and I'd ask the company what theirs is. To friends I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now. Still not much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think about whether I want to be a splicer when I'm thirty-two, or something that lasts. Five years is long enough that I'd hate myself if I spent it just hoping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the house plan on hold for a year or two, see how things move, and keep the deposit growing. I'd look at retraining, maybe a technical course in grid systems or robot maintenance, once I'd seen which courses actually led to jobs. Leo and I would probably push the wedding back but still plan it. In the first year after, I'd want to be doing whatever job checks or fixes the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but more in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see which courses lead to jobs. How long would you give it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A year, maybe. If I waited longer than that I'd be cutting it close. I'm cautious, not slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years buy you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A choice. With two years I'm just holding on. With five I can actually pick something and get trained before it hits.

S3.say: She'd ask the company what its plan is and tell friends five years is enough if you start now. She'd still say little online.
S3.think: She'd ask herself whether she wants to be a splicer at 32 or do something lasting. She'd hate herself for spending five years just hoping.
S3.do: Keeps the house on hold for a year or two while growing the deposit, and after about a year of checking, retrains in grid systems or robot maintenance. Pushes the wedding back but still plans it, aiming to move into a job checking or fixing the machines.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough that I'd hate myself if I spent it just hoping.
S3.fieldNote: Uma's cautious streak shows again, but she sets herself a one-year limit for deciding. The extra time gives her a real choice rather than just holding on. Family plans are delayed, not abandoned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, that's a different feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get ready, so let's do it properly. At work I'd push for training for the whole crew. With friends I'd say we've got time, don't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Leo and I would be all right. I'd be thirty-seven, still young enough to learn something new. Ten years means I can buy the house and still sleep at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd buy the house, probably the small one near the river. I'd start a part-time course in grid control after a year or two, once I saw which ones led somewhere. I'd use the AI tools more at work so I'm comfortable with them. We'd keep putting a bit into an index fund, so we own a tiny slice of what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's more of a background worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy the house. Isn't that a risk if your jobs go in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but you can't stop living for ten years. We'd buy small, so the payments are low. And we'd have a decade to pay a lot of it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra five years change, compared with the five-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets us live normally while we prepare. With five years we'd be in waiting mode. With ten we can get on with life and get ready at the same time.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare properly and push for training for her whole crew. With friends she'd say there's time and no need to panic.
S4.think: She and Leo would be all right, with her still young enough at 37 to learn something new. Ten years means they can buy the house and still sleep at night.
S4.do: Buys the small house near the river with low payments and starts a part-time grid control course after a year or two. Uses AI tools more at work and puts a bit into an index fund.
S4.quote: Ten years means I can buy the house and still sleep at night.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Uma lets life go on: the house is back on. She defends the decision sensibly, buying small and paying it down. She and Leo would plan for the future while still living normally.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits me and Leo at the same time with no time to switch. The scary part isn't losing my job, it's both of us losing ours in the same month. What would help is income support for a year or two while people retrain, and the company telling us early what's coming, not the week before.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to couples like us, both in trades. People think about one person's job, but most households have two. If both go at once, it's a different problem.

headlineQuote: The scary part isn't losing my job, it's both of us losing ours in the same month.
portrait: Uma Alvarez is a 27-year-old underground crew lead who splices big cables in vaults beneath the city centre and lives with her partner Leo, a commercial electrician. They've saved a good deposit for a house, and she uses AI tools now and then, always checking the book before she cuts. She is calm in the plateau and steady disruption, even happy to hand robots the grunt work, but anxious about AGI in two or five years because both their trade jobs could go at once. With ten years she would buy the house, retrain part-time and get on with life while she prepares.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and Leo could lose both their jobs at the same time with no time to switch.
whatWouldHelp: Income support for a year or two while people retrain, and early, honest notice from the company about what's coming.
